summary:
Mendoza is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework. Argentina's Law 26.743, approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and remains one of the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. It permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. A decree of 5 February 2025 restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The national protective machinery has been dismantled in part. The federal anti-discrimination institute INADI was abolished in 2024, and the 1% Trans Labor Quota had its hires dismissed.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a figure reported by Agencia Presentes on 19 March 2026 that represents a 62% increase year on year and a ten-year record, averaging one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, with beatings the main modality. Institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and 32% of 2025 incidents took place in police stations or prisons; 43% of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

No Mendoza-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern for transgender visitors is documented, and the province has no local reporting infrastructure capable of generating separate records. It therefore sits under the national figures rather than producing its own. Activists interviewed in April 2025 by the Washington Blade, dateline Buenos Aires, told the publication that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common under President Javier Milei and is worse still in interior provinces such as Mendoza that lack strong reporting infrastructure.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in that case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's statutory position and its documented practice have moved in opposite directions. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration despite the statute remaining in force, and the Observatorio's 2025 totals were described by Agencia Presentes as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the country.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, who was stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, said the national government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The concentration of recorded incidents inside police stations and prisons, combined with security-force personnel as the leading identified perpetrator group, places the risk at the point of contact with the state rather than only in private or street settings. A visitor who is stopped, detained or required to produce documents therefore faces exposure to the same institutional channel that accounts for a third of recorded cases.

Mendoza's position as an interior province with no independent monitoring body means national statistics are the only available indicator of conditions there, and activists specifically identified interior provinces as the places where police violence is least likely to be reported or recorded.
localsOnly:
Residents rather than visitors bear the direct effects of the 1% Trans Labor Quota decision, under which hires were dismissed, and of the abolition of INADI in 2024, which removed the federal body that handled discrimination complaints.

The decree of 5 February 2025 governing gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment for minors applies to residents' access to public and private care for adolescents, and legal experts have argued it is illegal and unconstitutional. The second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison affects detained residents directly, and 32% of the 227 recorded hate crimes of 2025 occurred in police stations or prisons.

Legal gender recognition remains available without surgery, hormones or a court order under Law 26.743, and marriage equality has been available since 2010. Anti-discrimination protection is assembled from national and provincial provisions rather than from a single institute, following the abolition of INADI.

Domestic reporting of hate crime rests on the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio and outlets such as Agencia Presentes. Institutional violence in that series rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and the province of Mendoza has no equivalent local observatory.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation challenging the decree of 5 February 2025 on gender-affirming care for minors is unresolved in the sources available here; legal experts petitioned the courts, but no ruling is recorded.

The 2025 hate-crime total of 227 incidents is a national figure. How those incidents distribute across provinces, and whether any were recorded in Mendoza specifically, is not sourced. Mendoza has no separate local record to check against the national series.

No sourced material covers entry or visa screening, identity-document or marker rules as applied at Argentine borders, restroom or facility access, or the practical availability of gender-affirming care in Mendoza's health services. Anything the record says about the province is inference from the national framework and from activists' testimony about interior provinces, not a Mendoza-specific finding.

Whether the travesticidio aggravating circumstance has been applied or rejected in other cases since the Supreme Court's ruling of 5 April 2025 is not addressed in the sources, and the long-term effect of that ruling on charging practice is unresolved.
